transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess... I guess they brought me in because of what happened at the warehouse. I work down at the freight depot, you know, moving materials, loading up the trucks, that sort of thing. It's usually pretty straightforward, but lately, I don't know, things have just been... different. Like, the other day, I was by the forklift, right? And I just—I just froze. I had my arms up like this, just stuck there for I don't even know how long. And the sounds, the beeping—beep, beep, beep—when the machinery backs up, I started copying it. I couldn't really help it, I was just making the sounds and doing the hand signals the foremen use, but I wasn't directing anyone. I was just doing it. And then with the boxes, I'm supposed to just stack them on the pallets, standard procedure, but I started moving them in these strange little patterns. It made sense to me at the time, the way they needed to be arranged, but everyone else was getting so mad. They were yelling at me, telling me to stop, telling me I was holding up the line, but I just kept doing it. I couldn't just stop, you know? The patterns had to be right, and the beeping... it's all just so loud there anyway, I don't see why me doing it too was such a big deal, but my manager got really upset and said I had to come here if I wanted to keep my job. So, here I am.
Have you ever felt like your body was stiff or frozen, even when you wanted to move, or found yourself repeating movements or sounds without meaning to?

Yeah, I mean, that's exactly what I was just trying to tell you about what happened at the depot. It's like... like my body just turns to cement, you know? Like I was just saying about the forklift, I was standing there, and my arms were up, just locked in place in the air. I wanted to put them down, I think, but they just wouldn't go. It was like they were made of lead or something, just completely stiff, and I was just stuck there while the whole warehouse was moving around me. 

And the sounds, yeah, exactly like I mentioned with the beeping... beep, beep, beep... it just comes out of my mouth. I hear the machinery, the big loaders backing up, and my mouth just starts making the exact same noise, and my hands are doing the signals the foremen use when they're guiding the trucks into the loading bay. I'm not trying to do it, it just happens, over and over, like an echo I can't swallow down. And then with the boxes, it's the same kind of thing. I get stuck doing those patterns I told you about, arranging them in these specific ways, and my hands just keep moving them back and forth into the exact spots. Even when the supervisor is right there in my face, literally screaming at me to stop and load the pallet normally so the truck can leave, I just can't. I just keep doing the patterns and making the sounds. It's like I'm stuck on a loop and I can't hit pause, even when everyone is yelling at me to snap out of it.
Do these experiences—feeling frozen, repeating sounds, or arranging things in certain patterns—ever happen to you when you're not at work, like at home or in other places?

No, not really. I mean, it's pretty much just at the depot. When I'm at home, in my apartment—I have this little place over on 4th Street, it's not much, just a one-bedroom, but it's quiet, you know? It's really quiet compared to the warehouse. At work, there's always something going on. The belts are moving, the trucks are idling, people are yelling over the noise of the forklifts... it's a lot of sensory input, just a constant barrage of noise and movement. But at home, it's just me. I don't really have the beeping to copy because there aren't any trucks backing up in my living room, obviously. 

And the freezing thing... I haven't noticed it happening when I'm just sitting on my couch watching TV or making dinner. I think maybe it has something to do with the pressure at work, or the environment, or maybe just the sheer volume of things happening around me that makes my brain just... stop. Or makes my body stop, I guess. Because at home, I can just sit there. I don't have a foreman breathing down my neck, telling me I'm holding up the line. I don't have to worry about the pallets being stacked exactly right for the manifest. It's just... still. So, no, I don't really find myself getting stuck like that or repeating things when I'm away from the job. It seems to be entirely tied to the depot and the freight and the machinery there. It's like that place just triggers something in me that makes me get stuck in those loops. But once I clock out and get on the bus and go home, it's like I can finally just be normal again. Well, as normal as I can be, anyway.
When you're at home, watching TV or doing everyday things, do you ever find yourself repeating words or phrases you hear, or mimicking movements you see, even a little bit?

No, no, I really don't. Like I said, it's just the warehouse. When I'm at home, I'm just... I'm just sitting there. I have this old TV, it's not a flat screen or anything, just one of those older boxy ones I got from a thrift store down the street a couple years ago, and I mostly just watch reruns. Sitcoms, mostly, because the laugh track is kind of soothing, you know? It's predictable. But I don't ever catch myself repeating what the actors are saying. I don't mimic them opening doors or sitting down on couches or anything like that. 

I might make a sandwich—usually just turkey and cheese, maybe some mayo if I have it, on wheat bread—and I just make it normally. I don't get stuck holding the knife in the air, I don't repeat the sound of the refrigerator humming. It's just me, eating my sandwich, watching my shows. Sometimes I'll read a little, I have some old textbooks from when I tried taking a few classes at the community college a while back. I thought about getting a degree in logistics, since I already work in freight, but it was just too much reading, and the tuition was getting crazy, so I dropped out after a couple semesters. Anyway, I might flip through those, but I don't get stuck turning the pages in patterns or anything. 

It really is just the depot. There's something about the depot, the sheer scale of it, the concrete floors, the metal racks going up thirty feet, the constant, never-ending noise of the diesel engines and the warning beeps and the foremen yelling about quotas... it's just a totally different world than my apartment. At home, I'm safe from all that. I can just breathe. I can just be me, without my body acting like it belongs to the forklift or the pallets. So, no, none of that stuff happens when I'm just hanging out at home watching TV or whatever. It's only when I punch that time card.
Have you ever noticed yourself repeating words or phrases you hear on TV, or copying movements you see others make, even slightly, like when you're watching a show or talking to someone?

Like I was just saying, no, not with the TV. Not with the sitcoms or anything like that. I mean, I feel like we're going in circles a little bit here, because I really don't do that stuff anywhere else but work. I guess... I mean, I guess the whole reason they even brought me in here to see you today, the reason I'm sitting in this office right now instead of finishing my shift on the docks, is entirely because of what I keep doing at the warehouse. It's always the warehouse. 

They brought me in because I keep doing those exact things there, like freezing completely solid with my arms up in the air right by the forklift, just like I was telling you about. Or copying the beeping sounds the trucks make and doing the hand signals the foremen use to guide them in. And the boxes, too... I just get stuck moving them in those strange little patterns, sliding them back and forth into these exact spots on the pallets, even when literally everyone around me is yelling for me to stop and just load the freight so the driver can leave. That's why I'm here. It's not because I'm sitting on my couch at home repeating lines from old TV shows or copying somebody at the grocery store. It's because the guys at the depot got freaked out when I got stuck in one of those loops again and wouldn't snap out of it when the supervisor was screaming right in my face. So, no, I don't do it watching a show. It's just the stuff at the depot. That's the whole reason this is even a thing they wanted me to get checked out for.
When you're talking to people, like coworkers or others outside of work, do you ever find yourself repeating their words or copying their movements, even if just slightly?

Look, Doc, I feel like you're asking me the exact same question again, just worded a little differently. Outside of work? No. Never. I already said that. But with my coworkers? I mean, I literally just explained this whole thing to you. 

The whole entire reason my boss had me brought in here today is because of what happens when I'm around those guys at the warehouse. But it's not like we're just standing around the breakroom chatting about the weekend and I start repeating their sentences like a parrot. It's out on the floor. Like I was just saying, I'll be right there by the forklift, and I'll just completely freeze up. My arms will get stuck up in the air like I'm holding a ghost box or something, and I'll start copying the sounds—the backup beeping sounds the machinery makes—and doing the exact hand signals the spotters use to guide the trucks in. 

And my coworkers, they'll be right there, practically right in my face, and they're literally yelling at me to snap out of it. They're screaming, "Stop! What are you doing? Just load the truck!" but I can't. I just keep moving the boxes in these strange little patterns, sliding them around into these specific spots on the pallet instead of actually loading them, completely ignoring everyone yelling for me to stop. I'm not copying *their* words when they yell, and I'm not copying *their* movements when they wave their hands in my face. I'm just stuck doing the warehouse stuff, the signals and the beeps and the box patterns. That's what I've been trying to tell you this whole time. It's not a conversation thing, it's a getting-stuck-at-the-depot thing. I really don't know how else to explain it to you.

Outside of the warehouse, do you ever notice yourself repeating words or copying movements in response to certain sounds, images, or sensations—like if you hear a specific noise or see something move a certain way?

Doc, seriously, are you writing any of this down? Because I feel like I'm losing my mind here, no offense. You keep asking me the exact same question about outside the warehouse. 'At home', 'watching TV', 'talking to people', and now 'hearing a specific noise outside'. No. No! How many times do I have to say it? 

If I'm walking down the street to get groceries and I hear a car horn, or like, an ambulance siren going by, I don't start mimicking it. If I see some guy waving down a bus on the corner, I don't copy his arm movements. I just walk. I just go about my day like a completely normal person. The sounds of the city, the traffic, the weather—none of that does anything to me. 

The whole reason I'm sitting in this chair, the absolute only reason management dragged me into this clinic today, is because of what happens specifically *at the warehouse*. It's the warehouse! I guess they brought me in because at the warehouse, I keep doing those exact things I literally just spent the last ten minutes telling you about. I freeze up. I will be standing right by the forklift, and my arms will just go up in the air, and I get completely stuck like that. Like a statue. And then I start copying the backup beeps the machinery makes, and doing the exact hand signals the spotters use to guide the freight in. 

Or I'll be at the pallets, and instead of actually loading the truck so the driver can get on the road and meet his quota, I'm just moving the boxes in these strange little patterns. Sliding them left, sliding them right, over and over, and my coworkers and the foremen are literally screaming at me to stop, yelling right in my face to just load the damn truck, and I just can't. 

It's the forklift. It's the boxes. It's the depot. It's not the grocery store, it's not my apartment, it's not a random noise on the street. I really, really need you to understand that, because if we keep talking about outside the warehouse, we're never going to figure out why the warehouse is doing this to me. Do you get what I'm saying? It's like a switch flips the second I punch my timecard. So no, nothing outside. Just the freezing and the beeping and the box patterns at work. That's it. That's the whole thing. I don't know how to make it any clearer.
When you're at the warehouse, do you ever feel like certain sounds or sights automatically make you repeat words or copy movements, like they pull the response out of you without you meaning to?

Yeah. Yes. Exactly. Finally, yes, that's exactly what it feels like. It's like... it's like I don't even have a choice in the matter. I'm not doing it on purpose to piss anybody off or ruin the shift, I promise you that. You walk into that place, and it's just this massive concrete cavern, right? The fluorescent lights are humming, the diesel engines are running, and there's just so much going on, so much noise and motion everywhere you look. And it's like those sounds and those sights just... they hijack my brain. They pull the actions right out of me before I even realize what's happening. 

I mean, I know that's exactly why they brought me in, because at the warehouse I just keep doing things like freezing completely solid with my arms up in the air right by the forklift the second I see it moving. I hear that backup alarm, that high-pitched beep-beep-beep, and see the yellow flashing lights, and it just forces me to start copying the beeping sounds and doing the exact hand signals the spotters use. I don't mean to do it! It just happens, like a reflex I can't control. 

Or I'll look at the freight, and the way the cardboard looks or the way the pallets are stacked just compels me, and I get stuck moving the boxes in these strange little patterns. I'll just be sliding them back and forth into these exact spots, over and over, and it's like I'm trapped inside my own body doing it, even when literally everyone around me is yelling for me to stop. They're screaming right in my face to snap out of it and load the truck, and I hear them, I really do, but the warehouse sounds and the shapes of the boxes just have this absolute grip on me, and I can't stop the patterns. It's like the building itself is just pulling all of it out of me like a puppet.

When you're at the warehouse, do the specific sounds like the forklift beeping or sights like the way the boxes are arranged automatically make you repeat the sounds or copy the movements, like they're pulling the actions out of you without you being able to stop them?

Doc, I... I feel like we're just going in circles now. I literally just said that. Yes. Yes, they pull it out of me. That's exactly it. That's the whole reason my foreman and management made me come here. I guess they brought me in because at the warehouse I just keep doing these things... these exact things we've been talking about for I don't know how long now. 

It's like... okay, picture the depot, right? It's huge, it's loud, the air smells like diesel and dust, and I'll be standing there in my steel-toes, and that forklift starts backing up. I see the yellow paint, I hear that *beep, beep, beep* echoing off the high corrugated ceilings, and it just... it takes over. I freeze. My arms go straight up by the forklift, completely stiff, and I'm copying the beeping sounds, making the exact same pitch with my mouth, doing the hand signals... and I can't put my arms down. I can't. Even if my muscles start burning, I'm just locked in.

And the boxes... it's the exact same thing with the freight. I look at the pallets, and the way the cardboard is stacked, the geometry of it or whatever, it just reaches into my brain and forces my hands to move. I end up moving the boxes in these strange little patterns, just sliding them around, lining up the corners perfectly, sliding them back, and it feels like the most important thing in the world in that exact second. And the whole time, my coworkers are literally right there, veins popping out of their necks, yelling for me to stop, screaming at me to just load the truck so we can make the outbound quota... and I can hear them, but I can't stop. The sights and the sounds just... they own my body in that moment. 

So yeah, it's automatic. I don't know how many more ways I can explain the exact same freezing and box patterns to you, man. I'm trying my best here, but it's just like I said—the warehouse pulls it out of me and I can't stop it.

When you're at the warehouse, does a specific sound or sight automatically make you repeat the sound or copy the movement, like the forklift beeping makes you beep or seeing a hand signal makes you copy it?

Doc... is there... is there a hidden camera in here or something? Seriously, man, are you messing with me right now? Because I feel like my brain is actually melting out of my ears. I literally *just* said that. Like, thirty seconds ago, I just gave you that exact answer. 

Yes! Yes, the forklift beeping makes me beep. Yes, seeing the spotter's hand signal makes me copy the hand signal. I don't... I don't know what else you want from me here. I don't have some other secret answer for you. I'm sitting here, you know, I took time off from my classes at the community college to work this freight job because the hourly was supposed to be good, and now I'm just stuck in this absolute nightmare loop. I'm stuck in a loop at work with the boxes and the machinery, and now I'm stuck in a loop in this office with you asking me the exact same question four times in a row! 

I don't know what else to tell you, man. I really don't. I haven't noticed it happening with anything else, if that's what you're digging for. I'm not... I'm not copying the sound of the vending machine in the breakroom. I'm not mimicking the sound of the timeclock punching my card. It's just the stuff I already spent the last twenty minutes practically begging you to understand. The yellow forklift. The high-pitched backup alarm. The spotters waving their arms. The cardboard pallets. That is what pulls it out of me. 

I don't have anything else to give you on this. That's all of it. I'm giving you everything I have. Can we please, please just move on and figure out how to make it stop? Because if I have to explain the forklift to you one more time, I'm going to lose whatever is left of my mind.
When you hear the forklift beeping or see someone making a hand signal at the warehouse, do you feel like you have to copy the sound or movement, like it’s something you can’t resist doing?

Doc, I swear to God, if you ask me about the forklift one more time... I already said yes! Yes, I can't resist it, yes, I copy the sounds and the hand signals, yes, it's automatic. I literally just spent twenty minutes explaining that to you! But you're missing the whole point of why I'm in so much trouble at the warehouse. It's not just the copying, it's what happens when I try to open my mouth to talk to anybody about it, or about anything at all on the floor. 

Like, okay, just listen to me for a second, please. Forget the forklift. Think about when my supervisor comes over. He comes over because I'm holding up the line, right? And he asks me a super simple question, like he just asks me which pallets are going on the outbound truck. That's it. And I have the load sheet right there in my hand, so I should just be able to read it. I look at the paper, and I start trying to explain the staging order to him, but my words just completely derail. 

I'll start talking about the load sheet, but then the splintered wood on the pallet makes me think of the deck at my old house, so suddenly I'm talking to my boss about the porch at my old house back when I was a kid. And then, before I can even catch myself, that jumps to fishing, because we used to keep all our rods and tackle boxes under that porch, so now I'm standing in the middle of a massive freight depot explaining bass fishing to my supervisor. And then from fishing, my brain just jumps straight to the wooden donation boxes at my church, and I just keep talking and connecting all these random things that are just flying out of my mouth at lightning speed. 

And my supervisor is just standing there staring at me with his mouth hanging open. He's looking at me like I'm an alien, because by the time I'm finally done talking, nobody—literally nobody, not the boss, not the spotters, not even me—knows what I meant. I was trying to tell him about the pallets for the truck, and I ended up giving a ten-minute speech about church boxes and fishing tackle. It's like my brain just shatters into a million pieces the second I try to explain anything, and the words just jump and jump and jump. So yeah, the forklift thing happens, but I can't even explain myself to management because my sentences won't stay in a straight line. Do you get what I'm saying? Because I really need you to hear me on this instead of asking about the backup alarm again.
When you're at the warehouse and you copy a sound or a movement, like the forklift beep or a hand signal, do you feel like you have to do it, like it’s something you can’t resist or control?

Are you... are you actually kidding me right now? Doc, did you even hear a single word I just said about the load sheets and my supervisor? You're asking me about the forklift again. I... I literally cannot believe this is happening. 

Yes! Yes, it's something I can't control! I mean, I guess they brought me in here, like management forced me to come to this clinic, specifically because at the warehouse I just keep doing these things. I'm out there on the floor freezing with my arms straight up by the forklift, copying the beeping sounds, copying the spotter's hand signals, and I can't just snap out of it. And it's the exact same deal with the freight—I'm moving the boxes in these strange little patterns, just sliding the cardboard around and lining up the edges over and over again, even when everyone is literally yelling for me to stop. 

My coworkers are standing right there screaming at me to just load the truck, the foreman is losing his mind because we're missing our outbound times, and I just keep doing it anyway because I can't resist it. I can't control my own hands or my own voice when it happens! I've told you this like five times now, man! The freezing, the copying, the weird box patterns... that's why I'm in trouble at work, and that's the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair talking to you. 

So yes, for the millionth time, I feel like I have to do it and I can't stop it. Can we please, please just move past the forklift now?
When you're at the warehouse and someone says something to you, like a command or a question, do you feel like you have to repeat their exact words, even if you don't want to?

Okay, wow. So... so now we're moving from the forklift beep to... what, me acting like a parrot? No, man. No. I don't repeat what people say to me. Like, if my supervisor—his name is Dave, by the way, he's this big guy who always looks like his blood pressure is completely through the roof—if Dave storms over and yells, 'Hey, get those boxes on the outbound truck!' I'm not standing there going, 'Hey, get those boxes on the outbound truck!' right back at his face. I'm not a toddler playing the mimic game. 

I told you, I get stuck on the sounds, the mechanical stuff, the high-pitched alarms, the hand signals from the spotters. But when people actually speak actual words to me? No, I don't repeat their sentences. If I did that, Dave probably would have actually knocked me out by now, because he's already on the absolute edge with the whole freezing thing and the cardboard sliding thing I do. 

When someone asks me a question or gives me a command, I try to answer them! I really do! But like I literally just spent a massive chunk of time explaining to you, when I try to answer, my brain goes from the load sheet to the splintered wood to the porch to the fishing tackle to the church boxes! I don't repeat *their* words, I just can't make *my own* words make any sense! It's like you're trying to put me in this specific little checklist you have on your clipboard, just throwing darts and hoping one of them sticks. 

I don't repeat people's words. I hear them, I understand they're furious with me because we're missing our times, I try to respond like a normal human being, and it just comes out as a giant, confusing mess about bass fishing. That's what happens with words. I don't copy them. Please, man, tell me you actually heard me this time.
When someone speaks to you at the warehouse, do you ever feel the need to repeat their exact words, even if you don't want to?

Are you... is this a prank? Is there like a two-way mirror in here with people watching? Because you literally just asked me that. You just asked me that exact same question not even two minutes ago! I just gave you this whole huge explanation about Dave, my supervisor, and how he'd probably punch me in the face if I stood there repeating his sentences back to him. 

No! The answer is still no! I don't repeat what people say. I don't know if you're testing my memory right now, or if you're just not writing anything down on that clipboard of yours, but it's making me feel like I'm completely losing my mind in this room. Like I just said, if someone walks up to me on the floor, like if one of the spotters says, hey man, where did you leave the pallet jack, I don't look at them and say, hey man, where did you leave the pallet jack. I don't do that! I try to answer them! I try to tell them it's over by the loading dock, but then my brain hears the word dock and suddenly I'm talking about the lake, and the boats, and the water, and everything else except the pallet jack. 

But I never, ever just repeat their words back to them. I don't mimic people. I mimic the forklift, yeah, I mimic the hand signals, I already admitted to all of that, but not actual human words. I really, really need you to actually listen to what I'm saying, man, because sitting here having to answer the exact same question twice in a row when I'm already this stressed out about losing my job is just... it's too much. I'm trying so hard to explain what's actually wrong with me. So no. I don't repeat people. Can we please move on to whatever the next thing on your list is?
When someone speaks to you outside of the warehouse, like a friend or a family member, do you ever feel the need to repeat their exact words, even if you don't want to?

Okay, so... you just changed the location. That's what we're doing now? We're just playing Mad Libs with your little clipboard? You're just swapping out 'warehouse' for 'outside the warehouse' and asking me the exact same thing for a third time? 

No! No, man! Not outside the warehouse either! Not with friends, not with family, not with the guy at the corner gas station! It is the exact same answer I just gave you, just in a different building! 

Like, look, I live with my buddy from college, right? We went to state together for a couple semesters before I had to drop out and take this freight job. His name is Mike. If I'm sitting on the couch and Mike comes in from work and says, 'Hey man, did you pay the electric bill?' I am not sitting there on the cushions looking up at him and saying, 'Hey man, did you pay the electric bill?' 

Why would I do that? I've never done that in my entire life! If he asks me about the electric bill, I try to say yes, I paid it online on Tuesday. But like I keep trying to explain to you—and I feel like I'm taking crazy pills because you just are not getting it—my brain doesn't let me answer straight! I try to say 'bill,' and then I think about dollar bills, and then George Washington, and then cherry trees, and then suddenly I'm rambling to Mike about planting fruit trees in the front yard and he's looking at me like my brain is completely broken. 

That is what happens! My own words get messed up. I don't steal *their* words! I don't care if it's Dave at the loading dock screaming about pallets, or Mike in our living room asking about the Wi-Fi, or my mom calling me on the telephone on a Sunday afternoon to ask how I'm doing. I don't repeat what people say. Period. Never. 

Can we please, please talk about something else now? Because asking me the exact same thing three times in a row just by changing the scenery is seriously making my chest tight, and I really need you to just write down 'no' and move to the next page.

When you're at the warehouse, do specific sounds or sights, like the forklift beeping or someone making a hand signal, make you repeat the sound or copy the movement automatically, without meaning to?

Yes! Okay, yes, finally, thank you! See, this is exactly what I was trying to tell you literally five minutes ago when you kept asking me about the parrot thing! 

Yes, the sounds and the movements. It's the mechanical stuff. Like, okay, at the warehouse we use these Yale reach trucks—they're the big yellow ones for the high racks—and whenever they go into reverse, they have this incredibly loud, piercing backup alarm. *Beep, beep, beep.* It just cuts right through the whole building. And I don't even think about it, I don't plan it, my mouth just starts making the exact same noise. It just comes out of my throat, matching the pitch perfectly. 

And it's the same with the sights, like the hand signals. The spotters, the guys walking around in the neon high-vis vests guiding the drivers... if one of them does the little twirl with his finger to tell the driver to wrap the pallet, my finger just instantly starts twirling. If they do the 'stop' motion, like throwing their hand flat out, my arm just shoots up and my hand goes flat out. 

And then... then I just get stuck. I'll just freeze like that. I'll literally freeze completely solid with my arms up right next to the forklift. Which is obviously insanely dangerous, right? Like, OSHA would have an absolute field day if they saw it, because you cannot just be standing paralyzed next to a five-ton machine moving freight, but I literally cannot put my arms down! I'm just stuck there like a statue. 

And it's not just the freezing or the mimicking, either. It's the boxes. My job is literally just taking boxes off the line and stacking them on the pallet, interlocking them so they don't tip over when we wrap them. Basic warehouse 101 stuff. But instead of just stacking them, I'll start moving them around into these strange little patterns on the floor. I'll be sliding the cardboard around, making these specific shapes or grids, and I have to do it, I have to finish the pattern. 

And the whole time, everyone is literally screaming at me. Dave is yelling, 'What are you doing, stop, load the outbound truck!' and the drivers are honking their horns, and the line is backing up, but I'm just down there sliding boxes into little squares or frozen with my hands in the air making backup noises. Honestly... I guess that's exactly why they brought me in here to see you in the first place. Because I keep doing all of that, and I just can't stop doing it, even when the entire dock is yelling for me to stop. So, yes. That. That is exactly what happens.

When you're at the warehouse, do specific non-verbal sounds or sights—like the forklift beeping or someone making a hand signal—automatically make you repeat the sound or copy the movement, even if you don't want to?

Are you... are you actually kidding me right now? Did you just read the exact same question off your paper again? Man, I... I literally just gave you a whole speech about this! Like, thirty seconds ago! I just told you all about the Yale reach trucks and the backup alarms and the spotters with their high-vis vests! I don't know if you're messing with me, or if your pen ran out of ink, or if you're just trying to see if my story changes, but I'll say it again if that's what it takes for you to actually check the box on your clipboard. 

Yes! Like I just said, I guess that is the whole entire reason they brought me in here to see you in the first place! Because at the warehouse, I keep doing these exact things. I'm out there on the floor, and I'll just be freezing completely solid with my arms up right by the forklift because I copied the spotter's hand signal, or I'm standing there copying the backup beeping sounds, or I'm down on the concrete moving the cardboard boxes into these strange little patterns instead of actually stacking them.

These behaviors are consistent with a diagnosis of schizotypal disorder with acute, transient, or brief psychotic-like episodes, but without a full-blown psychotic episode. The behaviors are not due to another mental disorder or neurological condition and are limited to a specific environmental context (the warehouse).
